opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something I've been thinking about a lot. Large language models are incredibly impressive, and I don't want to downplay that. But if you look at what they're actually doing, they're learning from text, which is a compressed, symbolic record of what humans have already figured out about the world. Language is a very efficient representation. Someone already did the hard work of perceiving the world, abstracting it, and writing it down, and the model learns from that output.

The real world doesn't come to you as tokens. It comes as a continuous, high-dimensional, noisy stream of sensory input: vision, sound, touch, physical feedback. An intelligence that actually lives in the world has to build its own abstractions from that raw signal. It has to understand space, objects, cause and effect, what happens if I push this thing or move over there. A lot of that knowledge is never written down, because to humans it's so obvious we never bother. A child learns that a cup falls when you let go long before they can say the word "gravity."

So when I make this distinction, I mean that LLMs are, in a sense, intelligence built on top of human knowledge. They're very good at manipulating and recombining what's already been articulated. Intelligence that interacts with the real world needs grounding. It has to perceive, predict, act, and learn from the consequences of its actions. That's where things like visual representation learning, world models, and embodiment come in.

I also think there's a question of where the next big leap comes from. Text data is finite, and we're starting to see the limits of just scaling on it. The visual and physical world is effectively unlimited in richness. If we want systems that can really reason about space, plan in physical environments, or eventually work alongside us as robots or agents in the real world, I don't think language alone gets us there. Language is a beautiful interface, but it's not the whole substrate of intelligence. Vision, and more broadly perception and interaction, is a much more fundamental part of the story, and I think as a field we've somewhat underinvested in it relative to how important it is.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text-based LLMs with real-world perception and interaction, but does not state that the problems current LLMs solve well predominantly occur in digital space.

fable-5.1.text:
When I draw that line, I'm really pointing at where the data comes from and what the model is actually being asked to do.

A large language model is trained on text, and text is already a compressed, human-produced abstraction of the world. Someone looked at something, thought about it, and wrote it down. So when a language model learns, it's learning from the residue of human intelligence. It's incredibly powerful, because language encodes an enormous amount of knowledge and reasoning patterns, but it's secondhand. The model never had to figure out what a cup is by seeing thousands of cups from different angles under different lighting. It just read the word "cup" next to other words.

Intelligence that interacts with the real world is a different problem. The input is raw. It's pixels, it's video, it's continuous sensory streams, and nobody has pre-labeled or pre-compressed that for you. A child doesn't learn to understand the physical world primarily through language. They learn it by watching, by moving, by seeing what happens when they push something off a table. Language comes later, on top of that foundation. Animals do this without language at all.

So the question I care about is whether we can build systems that learn a model of the world from that kind of raw observation, and then use language as an interface rather than as the source of their understanding. Right now a lot of the field is going the other way. We take a very strong language model and bolt a vision encoder onto it, and we get something that can describe an image quite well. But if you poke at it, you find it often doesn't really see. It's using language priors to guess what should be in the picture. It struggles with things like spatial relationships, counting, or fine details that are obvious to any person looking at the same image.

That gap is what I mean. Being able to talk about the world fluently is not the same as perceiving and understanding it. And I think the next real step, whether you call it embodied AI or world models or spatial intelligence, has to start from the visual side, from the sensory side, and build up. Not start from text and hope the perception fills in.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs are trained on text and contrasts that with raw sensory input, but it does not state that the problems current LLMs solve well predominantly occur in digital space.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is between learning from descriptions of the world and learning through interaction with the world. Language contains an enormous amount of human knowledge, so predicting language can take you surprisingly far. But if a model can describe how to pick up a cup, that doesn’t necessarily mean it can pick up a cup.

When you interact with the physical world, you have to perceive what’s happening, take an action, and then deal with the consequences. Maybe the cup is heavier than you expected, or it slips. You need to use that feedback to adjust. It’s a continuous loop between perception and action.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply between language models and robots. A language model could be part of a system that interacts with the world. The question is whether the system’s understanding is grounded in observations and actions, and whether it can learn when the world responds differently from what it predicted. That’s a broader challenge than producing a convincing answer.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from language with interacting with the physical world, but does not state that the problems current LLMs solve well predominantly occur in digital space.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is about how a system learns and what it can do with that knowledge. An LLM learns primarily from descriptions of the world. That’s incredibly powerful, because language contains so much of what humans have discovered. But describing an action and actually taking that action are different things.

If you’re a robot trying to pick up a cup, you need to understand where it is, how to move toward it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it slips. You act, observe the consequences, and adjust. Your actions change what you see next. That feedback loop is a central part of intelligence in the real world.

So I wouldn’t say language models aren’t intelligent. The question is whether learning from language alone gives you everything you need. To me, the interesting direction is connecting that ability to reason with perception and action, so a system can test its understanding against the world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from language with acting in the physical world, but does not state that current LLMs’ strongest problems predominantly occur in digital space.
